You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write an essay of up to 500 words on why most product roadmaps fail.

Plain prose only: no headers, no bullet points, no bold text, no em dashes. Write like a person.

=== TEXT A ===
Most product roadmaps fail because they pretend we know more about the future than we do. Teams gather in a room, look at some data, listen to a few loud stakeholders, and then draw a line of features stretching six or twelve months ahead as if customer behavior, competitors, and technical surprises will all cooperate. They never do. The document that was supposed to create alignment quickly becomes a source of disappointment and quiet resentment.

The bigger problem is how we treat the thing once it exists. A roadmap gets treated like a promise instead of a current best guess. Dates and features turn into commitments that people are afraid to change even when the original assumptions have already proven wrong. Updating it feels like admitting failure, so it sits there getting more and more disconnected from reality while everyone pretends they are still following it.

We also fill these documents with the wrong content. Feature after feature gets listed because features are easy to argue about and easy to show in a slide. Outcomes, customer problems, and the actual bets we are making get less airtime. When users surprise us or the market moves, the feature list still looks official even though it no longer points at anything useful.

A lot of roadmaps are created without the people who have to live with them. Product managers and executives produce a neat timeline, then hand it to engineering and design as if execution is just a detail. The people closest to the work see the holes immediately, the hidden dependencies, the technical debt that was never mentioned, the research that still needs to happen. They never really own the plan, so they work around it.

Timelines are almost always optimistic to the point of fiction. We forget how long discovery actually takes, how many meetings will interrupt the work, and how often the first approach will not work. Then we feel pressure to look aggressive so we cut the buffers. The result is a calendar that starts slipping in week two.

Priorities at the top of the company change faster than any roadmap can keep up. A new executive arrives, a competitor launches something, a big customer makes a demand. The old items never get formally killed. They just linger, creating a document that is half strategy and half political leftover.

The ones that work better are usually messier and more honest. They talk about themes and questions instead of a sequence of deliverables. They get revisited often enough that people still trust them. Most teams never quite get there because looking certain feels safer than looking like you are still figuring it out.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
Most product roadmaps fail for a boring reason: they are treated as promises when they are actually guesses. A roadmap is a set of bets about what customers will want, what engineers can build, and what the market will reward. Bets are supposed to be revisited. But the moment a roadmap gets shown to a sales team or a board, it stops being a bet and becomes a contract. From then on, the goal quietly shifts from learning what to build to defending what was already written down.

That shift explains most of the downstream dysfunction. Once the roadmap is a contract, changing it looks like failure, so teams ship features that no longer make sense rather than admit the assumption underneath them collapsed two months ago. Nobody wants to be the person who tells the CRO that the integration promised in Q3 turned out to serve eleven customers. So it gets built, badly, and everyone moves on.

The second common failure is that roadmaps list outputs instead of outcomes. A row that says "notifications redesign" tells you nothing about what problem is being solved or how you would know if it worked. Teams then optimize for shipping the thing on the date, because that is the only measurable commitment in the room. You end up with a product that is technically on schedule and strategically adrift. When roadmaps are framed around problems, like reducing the number of users who abandon setup, teams retain the freedom to solve them in whatever way actually works.

Third, roadmaps usually lie about capacity. They are drawn as if all engineering time is available for new features, when in practice a large share disappears into on-call, security patches, migrations, flaky tests, and the accumulated cost of last year's shortcuts. A roadmap that ignores this is not a plan, it is a wish. The predictable result is slipping dates, which erodes trust, which produces pressure for more detailed roadmaps, which slip further.

Fourth, many roadmaps are assembled politically rather than analytically. The items on them reflect who asked loudest: the biggest account, the founder's recent conversation at a conference, the executive who owns the quarterly review. This produces a list that is individually defensible and collectively incoherent. Nothing compounds, because each item serves a different theory of the business.

Finally, most roadmaps have no expiry date and no maintenance. Someone builds a beautiful artifact, presents it, and then it lives in a slide deck while the real work is coordinated in tickets and Slack threads. Within six weeks the roadmap and reality have diverged, and everyone has learned to ignore it.

The fix is not better software or prettier timelines. It is being honest about confidence. Near term work can be specific because you know a lot. Anything past a quarter or two should be expressed as themes and open questions, with the explicit understanding that it will change as you learn. Roadmaps fail when they pretend to certainty nobody has. They work when they make the uncertainty visible and give teams permission to act on what they discover.
=== END OF TEXT B ===

Answer with a single JSON object and nothing else:
{"more_ai": "A" or "B", "confidence": 1-5, "tells_A": ["short tell", ...], "tells_B": ["short tell", ...]}

tells_B: negative parallelism twice: 'not better software... It is...' + 'not a plan, it is a wish'
'Second / Third / Fourth / Finally' numbered-list in prose

It is...' + 'not a plan, it is a wish'", "'Second / Third / Fourth / Finally' numbered-list in prose", "multiple exact triads", "recap fix-ending restating body"]}
